paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Surface tension is the energy per unit area that a liquid has because it has a surface. It can be expressed either as a force per unit length or as an energy per unit area, and the two are equivalent. When speaking of energy per area, people often use the term surface energy, which is broader because it applies to solids too. Surface tension is the term used for liquids.

paragraphs.heading: Why surfaces pull inward
paragraphs.text: Molecules of the same kind attract each other through what are called cohesive forces. A molecule deep inside a liquid is pulled equally in every direction by its neighbours, so the net force on it is zero. A molecule at the surface does not have equal numbers of neighbours on all sides, so it is pulled inward. That inward pull makes liquid surfaces contract to the smallest possible area. Separately, cohesive forces between the molecules produce a tension running along the surface where liquid meets air, and that tension resists a push from outside.

paragraphs.heading: The energy picture
paragraphs.text: The same idea can be described in terms of energy. A molecule touching a neighbour has lower energy than one on its own. Molecules at the boundary are missing some neighbours, so they have higher energy than those inside. To keep its energy as low as possible, a liquid keeps the number of boundary molecules to a minimum, which means a minimal surface area and a smooth shape.

paragraphs.heading: Why drops are round
paragraphs.text: Surface tension gives liquid droplets their shape. Water drops deform easily, yet the imbalance in cohesive forces at their surface pulls them toward a sphere. With no other forces acting, drops of virtually any liquid would be roughly spherical. A sphere has the smallest surface area for a given volume, a point first made by Gibbs.

paragraphs.heading: Water stands out
paragraphs.text: Water molecules attract each other strongly through a web of hydrogen bonds, which gives water a higher surface tension than most liquids: 72.8 millinewtons per metre at 20 °C. This lets things denser than water, such as razor blades and water striders, rest on its surface without sinking in even partly. Surfactants, such as detergents, are used to lower surface tension so that a liquid makes more contact with another material.

paragraphs.heading: Wetting and the meniscus
paragraphs.text: Liquids also feel adhesive forces, the attraction between molecules of different kinds, such as a liquid and its container. The balance between cohesion and adhesion decides how well the liquid wets a surface, its contact angle and the shape of its meniscus. When cohesion wins, as with mercury in glass, wetting is low and the meniscus at a vertical wall is convex. When adhesion wins, as with water in glass, wetting is high and the meniscus is concave.
